title: Biological Oscillators
markdown: ## What this covers Some biochemical networks do not settle to a steady concentration — they oscillate forever, tracing a closed loop in concentration space. This chapter asks what has to be true of the rate equations for that to happen, and answers it with two examples: a generic two-variable network whose fixed point can be pushed from a stable spiral into a limit cycle, and the repressilator, a three-gene ring that Elowitz and Leibler actually built in *E. coli* to test the idea. It assumes the linear stability machinery from earlier in the course — nullclines, the Jacobian at a fixed point, and the trace/determinant classification of a 2D linear system (stable node, stable spiral, saddle, unstable spiral) — and only extends that machinery to the point where a fixed point loses stability and a cycle is born around it. ## A generic two-variable oscillator Take a network of two species with the rate equations $$ \dot x = -x + ay + x^2y, \qquad \dot y = b - ay - x^2y . $$ The $x^2y$ term is autocatalytic in $x$: production of $x$ accelerates as $x$ itself accumulates, which is the ingredient that makes oscillation possible at all in a two-variable system. The nullclines ($\dot x=0$ and $\dot y=0$) are $$ y = \frac{x}{a+x^2}, \qquad y = \frac{b}{a+x^2}, $$ and since both have the same denominator, they cross where $x = b$ — a single fixed point, $$ x^\ast = b, \qquad y^\ast = \frac{b}{a+b^2}. $$ **The Jacobian.** Differentiating the right-hand sides and evaluating at $(x^\ast,y^\ast)$ gives $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1+2x^\ast y^\ast & a+(x^\ast)^2 \\ -2x^\ast y^\ast & -\left(a+(x^\ast)^2\right) \end{bmatrix}. $$ Notice the two columns are unrelated, but the two entries of each *row* pair up in a way that costs nothing to check: adding the two equations gives $\dot x + \dot y = b - x$, a relation that depends on $x$ alone. That forces the row sums of $A$ to reproduce $\partial(b-x)/\partial x = -1$ and $\partial(b-x)/\partial y = 0$, i.e. the first row of $A$ sums to $-1$ and the second sums to $0$. Using the second of these to eliminate $A_{22}=-A_{12}$ from the determinant collapses it to $$ \Delta = \det A = a + (x^\ast)^2 = a+b^2 \;>\;0 \quad \text{always.} $$ So this fixed point is *never* a saddle: it is always some kind of node or spiral, and whether it is stable or unstable is decided purely by the sign of the trace, $$ \tau = \operatorname{tr} A = -\frac{b^4+(2a-1)b^2+(a+a^2)}{a+b^2}. $$ The fixed point is a stable spiral when $\tau<0$, and it turns into an unstable spiral — surrounded, once the nonlinear terms are accounted for, by a stable limit cycle — exactly when $\tau$ changes sign. That sign change, at fixed $\Delta>0$, is a Hopf bifurcation: a pair of complex eigenvalues crossing the imaginary axis. Setting $\tau=0$ and solving the resulting quadratic in $b^2$ shows the crossing only has real solutions when $a<\tfrac18$; for $a>\tfrac18$ the trace never changes sign and the fixed point is stable for every $b$. For $a<\tfrac18$ there are two roots $b_1(a) The lecture demonstrated this numerically rather than just analytically, integrating the ODE and plotting the trajectory in the $(x,y)$ plane: ```matlab % filename: cyclefunc.m function dydt = f(t,y,flag,a,b) dydt = [-y(1)+a*y(2)+y(1)*y(1)*y(2); b-a*y(2)-y(1)*y(1)*y(2)]; plot(y(1),y(2),'.'); drawnow; hold on; axis([0 2 0 2]); ``` ```matlab % filename: limitcycle.m close; clear; a=0.1; b=0.5; options=[]; [t y]=ode23('cyclefunc',[0 50],[0.6 1.4],options,a,b); plot(y(:,1),y(:,2)); ``` With $a=0.1,\,b=0.5$ — inside the tongue above — the trajectory spirals outward from the initial condition $(0.6,1.4)$ and settles onto a closed orbit: the limit cycle predicted by $\tau>0$. ## The repressilator: a synthetic genetic oscillator Elowitz and Leibler built a genetic oscillator "from scratch" in *E. coli*, using three repressor genes wired so that each represses the next (M. B. Elowitz and S. Leibler, *A synthetic oscillatory network of transcriptional regulators*, Nature **403**, 335–338, 2000). Writing the mRNA of gene $i$ as $m_i$ and its protein as $p_i$, with $i=[\text{lacI},\text{tetR},\text{cI}]$ repressed respectively by $j=[\text{cI},\text{lacI},\text{tetR}]$, $$ \frac{dm_i}{dt} = -m_i + \frac{\alpha}{1+p_j^{\,n}} + \alpha_o, \qquad \frac{dp_i}{dt} = -\beta(p_i-m_i). $$ Matching $i$ against $j$ gives the ring lacI $\dashv$ tetR $\dashv$ cI $\dashv$ lacI — each gene repressing the one after it, so that going once around the loop applies the repression three times. Collapsing the mRNA step (treating protein production as directly rate-limited by the repressor, with time measured in units of the protein decay rate) leaves three coupled equations, $$ \frac{dp_1}{dt} = -p_1+\frac{\alpha}{1+p_3^{\,n}}+\alpha_o, \quad \frac{dp_2}{dt} = -p_2+\frac{\alpha}{1+p_1^{\,n}}+\alpha_o, \quad \frac{dp_3}{dt} = -p_3+\frac{\alpha}{1+p_2^{\,n}}+\alpha_o . $$ If all three genes carry the same basal rate $\alpha_o$, maximum rate $\alpha$ and Hill coefficient $n$, there is a symmetric steady state $p\equiv p_1=p_2=p_3$ satisfying $$ p = \frac{\alpha}{1+p^n}+\alpha_o . $$ **The Jacobian is circulant.** Each equation depends on exactly one other variable — the one that represses it — so the Jacobian at the symmetric point has $-1$ on the diagonal and a single off-diagonal entry per row, cyclically permuted: $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & X \\ X & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & X & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad X \equiv -\frac{\alpha n p^{\,n-1}}{(1+p^n)^2} \;(\,\le 0\,), $$ $X$ being the (negative) slope of the repression function at the fixed point. The characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ reduces, using the cyclic symmetry, to $$ -(1+\lambda)^3 + X^3 = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (1+\lambda)^3 = X^3 . $$ A cube has three cube roots, so $1+\lambda$ must equal $X$ times one of the three cube roots of unity, $1,\ e^{2\pi i/3},\ e^{-2\pi i/3}$: $$ \lambda_1 = X-1, \qquad \lambda_{2,3} = -1-\tfrac12 X \pm i\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}X . $$ **Which root binds.** The real root $\lambda_1=X-1$ is always negative, since $X\le0$ — it can never destabilize the fixed point. The complex pair has real part $-1-\tfrac12X$, which turns positive once $X<-2$. So the *only* way this fixed point loses stability is through the complex pair crossing the imaginary axis — a Hopf bifurcation again, this time produced by a ring of three degradation equations rather than a two-variable phase plane. The full stability condition, combining both roots, is $$ -2-2$). The fixed point is stable whenever this holds. It oscillates in the complementary region — sufficiently cooperative repression (large Hill coefficient $n$) or a sufficiently strong promoter (large $\alpha$) makes the loop gain, $|X|$, large enough at the fixed point to push the complex eigenvalue pair across zero, and a limit cycle appears around it. Mechanically this is the same criterion as in the two-variable model: a pair of complex eigenvalues crossing the imaginary axis while the third stays put on the negative real axis. ## Exercises The following problems (MIT 8.591J, 2014 problem set 10) work through the same theme — when deterministic and stochastic population models oscillate — in settings beyond the two worked examples above: a system with neutral cycles rather than a limit cycle, oscillations that appear only because of demographic noise, a bifurcation into bistability, chaos in discrete time, and an epidemic threshold on a network. **1. Neutral cycles in the Lotka–Volterra model.** The non-dimensionalized Lotka–Volterra equations are $$ \frac{du}{dt} = u(1-v), \qquad \frac{dv}{dt} = \alpha v(u-1). $$ It was claimed in the lecture that these oscillations are neutrally stable, though in principle the nonlinear terms could turn them into a stable spiral or a genuine limit cycle. Show this claim is correct. a. Show that the fixed point of the *linearized* system is neutrally stable. b. Show that $H = \alpha u+v-\ln(u^\alpha v) = \alpha[u-\ln u]+[v-\ln v]$ is a constant of motion. c. Solutions require $H>H_{\min}$. Find $H_{\min}$. d. Show that, for fixed $H$, the prey population $u(t)$ is bounded between some $u_{\min}$ and $u_{\max}$. e. Explain why a constant of motion together with this bound implies that predator and prey trace out closed orbits. f. On the $(u,v)$ phase plane, sketch orbits for two values $H_10,\ N\ge0. $$ a. Show this captures the Allee effect described above. b. Take $r=2ab^2$. How many fixed points are there, and what is the stability of each? c. As environmental deterioration lowers $r$, find the critical value $r_1^{\text{critical}}$ at which the system becomes bistable. Name the type of bifurcation. d. If $r$ keeps decreasing, find $r_2^{\text{critical}}$ at which the system becomes monostable again. What is the surviving state, and what type of bifurcation is this? e. Find the eigenvalue at the nonzero stable fixed point as a function of $r$, and describe its behaviour as $r\to r_2^{\text{critical}}$. What does that imply about the recovery time after a small perturbation, and how might this serve as an early-warning signal of an impending population collapse? f. Sketch the bifurcation diagram — fixed-point position against $r$ — marking which branches are stable and which are unstable. **4. Time is discrete: the logistic map and chaos.** The continuous logistic equation $dN/dt=rN(1-N/K)$ has a discrete-time analogue, the logistic map $x_{t+1}=Rx_t(1-x_t)$. a. With $R=2$, plot $x_t$ for $20$ steps starting from $x_0=0.2$ and again from $x_0=0.99$. What kind of behaviour do you see across different initial values in $(0,1)$? b. With $R=3.1$, $x_0=0.2$, plot $20$ steps. How does the trajectory differ from part (a)? c. With $R=3.5$, $x_0=0.2$, plot $20$ steps. What is the oscillation period now? d. Find a value of $R$ that gives period $8$. e. Each of these transitions is a period-doubling bifurcation; further increasing $R$ produces deterministic chaos. Set $R=4$ and plot $80$ steps starting from $x_0=0.2$ and from $x_0=0.2000000001$ on the same graph. Do the two trajectories show sensitive dependence on initial conditions? **5. SIS on a network.** In the SIS (Susceptible–Infectious–Susceptible) model, individuals sit on the nodes of a network and each node holds some population. a. Let $S_t$, $I_t$ be the susceptible and infectious densities on the network at time $t$, and $p_I$ the probability a susceptible individual is infected by a given infectious neighbour. Assuming node degree is Poisson-distributed with mean $\langle d\rangle$, show that the probability a randomly chosen susceptible individual becomes infected at time $t$ is $P_t = 1-\exp(-p_I I_t\langle d\rangle)$. b. Suppose $I_t+S_t=\rho$ at every generation $t$, and $p_R$ is the probability an infectious individual recovers each generation. Write $I_{t+1}$ as a function of $I_t$. c. In the long-time limit $I_t=I_{t+1}=I_\infty$. Under what condition does $I_\infty=0$ stop being stable, so that the system settles into an endemic state instead? Find the threshold value of $\rho$ at which this transition occurs, and describe how the threshold depends on $\langle d\rangle$. ## Sources - **Slide/outline** — `lecture-outlines/10-outline.md` (MIT OCW 8.591J, 2004; the exposition of the two-variable oscillator, equations VII.1–VII.5, the MATLAB code, and the repressilator analysis, equations VII.6–VII.16, are taken from this outline throughout). The outline is a model reconstruction of a PDF with no text layer; every displayed equation there is flagged unverified, and this chapter's re-derivations of the trace/determinant formula and the circulant-matrix eigenvalues (via the cube roots of unity) were checked independently against the stated equations and are consistent with them. No lecture transcript or recording was supplied for this lecture. - **Referenced but not contained in the supplied material**: the phase-plane analysis of an earlier lecture ("L9_notes.pdf" in the outline) that first showed this system oscillating; the general linear-stability framework the outline calls "section V" (the Jacobian and eigenvalue conditions used without re-derivation here); the two figures extracted from page 2 of the source PDF (the phase portrait and the $(a,b)$ stability diagram the outline calls "Fig. 10" and "Figure 11"), which exist as image files but are not reproduced here — the parameter-plane figure above is redrawn directly from the trace formula in the outline, not from those image files; and the primary source, M. B. Elowitz and S. Leibler, *A synthetic oscillatory network of transcriptional regulators*, Nature **403**, 335–338 (2000). - **Exercises** — MIT OCW 8.591J (2014), problem set 10, questions 1–5, at `psets/10-questions/01-…` through `05-…`. These accompany the same theme (oscillation in population and epidemic models) but extend beyond this lecture's two worked examples into material — Lotka–Volterra neutral cycles, demographic-noise-driven oscillation, the Allee effect, the logistic map, and network SIS — presumably covered elsewhere in the course; they are included here because they were supplied as this chapter's problem set. Question 2 cites McKane and Newman, *Predator–Prey Cycles from Resonant Amplification of Demographic Stochasticity*, Phys. Rev.
